items.titleEn: Blue Jays unable to sweep, lose WC ground despite encouraging series
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- If the Blue Jays can reel off six more series like this to end the season, they’re headed to the postseason, but they couldn’t stick the landing for a sweep. ​

Sunday’s 6-1 loss to the Royals nudged the Blue Jays back to .500 and one game out of the final AL Wild Card spot, which now belongs to the Guardians again. The Blue Jays just beat those same Guardians and hold the season tiebreaker (4-2), but Cleveland has three walk-offs in their past three days.
This is what mattered most from Sunday in Kansas City:
1. Blue Jays still need more from Spencer Arrighetti
We can consider Arrighetti to be stretched all the way back out to a “starter” at this point, after throwing 91 pitches over 4 2/3 innings. Now, the Blue Jays need some quality out of those innings.

Arrighetti got rocked in the first, allowing a bunt single and walk to snowball when he served up a three-run shot to Vinnie Pasquantino. Salvador Perez later took him deep, too, and while Arrighetti allowed six runs, that number could have been even higher with all of the warning-track shots he gave up.

Better outings from Arrighetti aren’t a “want” for the Blue Jays, they’re a need. With Jameson Taillon back on the Blue Jays’ crowded IL, they’re stuck using a bullpen day as their No. 5 starter, which makes Arrighetti the No. 4. There’s no skipping him, but next time through, the Blue Jays may consider using an opener in front of Arrighetti.
2. The Adventures of Jesús Sánchez
How much longer can the Blue Jays run the risk of Jesús Sánchez roaming the outfield?

Sunday brought another glaring error when Sánchez dropped a simple fly ball in the second inning, which extended the inning for Arrighetti and cost him five more pitches. The odd blunder is excusable over 162 games, but these have become too common for Sánchez.

Out of 146 qualified outfielders, Sánchez is near the bottom with a -8 Fielding Run Value, metrically the weakest defender on a team that’s otherwise been among baseball’s best. This is actually a bit surprising for Sánchez, who had typically been closer to a league-average defender before being traded to the Blue Jays. This season, with a combination of physical and mental errors, it’s just not working.

The alternative is to have Myles Straw in left field, trading some offensive upside for much stronger defense and better speed. Given that the Blue Jays still profile as a lower-scoring team needing to win some tight games down the stretch, Straw makes a lot of sense in these spots. It could also leave the Blue Jays more willing to roll the dice on Sean Keys, who played just a handful of games in left field in Triple-A, but offers greater power upside than Sánchez and should be able to at least meet his 2026 standard defensively.
3. One bright spot: Josh Smith

Quietly, Smith has been one of the Blue Jays’ hottest hitters lately. His home run Sunday was his fourth in 18 games with the organization, too, a welcome sign in a lineup looking for a spark each night.
The Smith deal wasn’t the flashiest move of the Trade Deadline, coming over from the Rangers for lefty Adam Macko, but it’s working.

“When we acquired him, it was under the radar,” manager John Schneider said. “We still think he’s a good player who was having a down year. There are some things, mechanically, for him to get back to. He was aware of that, too. … He made some pretty quick adjustments.”

Immediately, Smith identified a disconnect between his upper and lower half. With that wrinkle smoothed out again, he’s unlocking better bat speed, and if he keeps hitting like this, he could force his way into the lineup more often down the stretch.
items.author: Keegan Matheson

items.titleEn: Okamoto's career-high 4-hit night fuels Blue Jays' burst above .500
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- Can you believe it? The Blue Jays, just 19 games from the finish line, own the final postseason spot in the American League.

Saturday’s 4-3 win over the Royals moved the Blue Jays into a tie for the final AL Wild Card spot with the Guardians, but they hold that tiebreaker based on their head-to-head record this season (4-2).

The win also moved the Blue Jays to 72-71. Yes, the number on the left is finally bigger than the one on the right. For the first time since April 3, when the Blue Jays were 4-3, they’re back above .500.
“Feels like it’s been a while, but I love the way we’re playing,” manager John Schneider said. “Love the way we’re being resilient. We struck first, got punched back in the mouth and stayed on it.”
This is what mattered most:
1. Kazuma Okamoto: The complete package
This may have been the best night of Okamoto’s big league career, his first four-hit performance with two runs driven in.

Okamoto did it all, from his classics to some new material. There were two doubles, including one ripped just inches inside the third-base line, and that’s what we’re used to seeing from Okamoto. Everything he hits is hard, and just about everything he hits is yanked to the left side of the diamond. Oddly enough, though, Okamoto’s most impressive swing of the night may have been the sixth-inning single, which he shot out to right-center field, which is rare territory for the Japanese slugger.

Okamoto’s game is built on highs and lows. On one hand, he’s struck out 167 times, just three shy of the Blue Jays’ all-time franchise record shared by Jose Bautista (2017) and Matt Chapman (‘22). The trade-off has been Okamoto’s power, though, with 28 home runs.

“There have been some ups and downs,” Okamoto said through interpreter Yusuke Oshima. “I know my weaknesses, but I’m always working to make sure that I can hit the ones I’m having a hard time hitting.”

Okamoto cannot be turned into a contact hitter, and thankfully, the Blue Jays haven’t whispered that idea. They’ve let him lean into his incredible natural power, and while everyone involved understands that will come with some empty at-bats in between, Saturday showed us the next level of Okamoto. When he’s at his best, Okamoto isn’t just a complementary power bat, he can change games.
“We’ve come this far, so all we can do is win and hopefully go to the postseason,” Okamoto said. “That’s all we’re thinking about. Every game, we’re giving it our all.”
2. Max Scherzer keeps the fight alive

All the Blue Jays needed from Scherzer was “enough,” and that’s exactly what he gave them. Allowing just three runs over 5 2/3 innings, Scherzer kept the Blue Jays in the game just long enough and gave the bullpen just enough help -- another solid day from the 42-year-old.

“I feel great. My body’s really responding. I’m getting stronger every outing and I’m executing better,” Scherzer said. “Outside of the first inning, I felt like I did a pretty good job. Let’s keep this going. I feel healthy, I feel good, everything’s in a good spot. Keep it going.”

Scherzer’s late-season run is one of the best stories we’ve seen this season. Now past his thumb, forearm, ankle and back issues, Scherzer is helping keep this rotation together with Dylan Cease and José Soriano as the only other healthy, full-length starters.
From there? It’s scramble mode, but the Blue Jays don’t want to mess with Scherzer’s schedule.
“As of now, we’re trying to keep Max where he is and have him go after the [Thursday] off-day,” Schneider said. “We’ll cross that bridge after we get through tomorrow.”
3. The path forward: Going for the sweep
It’s scoreboard-watching season, and starter Spencer Arrighetti will try to lead the Blue Jays to a sweep against Randy Dobnak in Sunday's finale.

If you’re a Blue Jays fan, you’ll spend one more day pretending to be a Red Sox fan, where lefty Payton Tolle takes on the Orioles. The Blue Jays and Orioles still have six games against one another, so it’s important that the Blue Jays create a bit of a gap there to eliminate the risk of a run.
The Guardians, though, have Gavin Williams, who mowed down 13 Blue Jays batters this past Tuesday, so the AL Wild Card rival is positioned well against the Tigers.
items.author: Keegan Matheson

items.titleEn: Taillon (right elbow inflammation) back on injured list
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- Jameson Taillon left Friday night’s start with right elbow discomfort, another setback just two innings into his first start back from the 15-day IL.

Taillon had been down with right forearm tendinitis, but he and the Blue Jays felt they’d caught that early, and he felt comfortable through a Triple-A rehab start before coming back to the big leagues. After just 29 pitches Friday night, though, John Schneider came out of the dugout to speak to the umpiring crew between innings while the bullpen quickly began to stir.
Taillon is now headed for an MRI after the Blue Jays’ 9-2 win over the Royals, and the club should have more information on Taillon this weekend.

“He said it felt a bit more nerve-y, if that makes sense,” John Schneider said. “He’s been through this a little bit and he said this felt a little bit different than the previous injury, so we’ll just see what the MRI says.”

This is a troubling blow to Taillon, the well-liked right-hander who is now in his 10th MLB season. After Taillon was designated for assignment by the Cubs just over a month ago, he was traded to the Blue Jays and immediately profiled as a rotation fill-in following the trade of Kevin Gausman. That hasn’t happened, though, and with so many injuries elsewhere in this rotation, the Blue Jays are back to scrambling.
Where does the rotation stand?

Dylan Cease is going to pitch every fifth day down the stretch, and with off-days each of the next three Thursdays, the Blue Jays can pull that off to maximize their ace’s value. The same could go for José Soriano, too, and if Max Scherzer feels strong, keep the trio rolling.

Beyond that, it’s messy. The Blue Jays have long been without José Berríos (Tommy John) and Cody Ponce (ACL). Even Bowden Francis (Tommy John) would have seen plenty of starts by now, but he was lost for the season. Shane Bieber is on the IL with right teres major inflammation, and Trey Yesavage underwent surgery to repair the meniscus in his left knee, but is chasing a comeback by the end of the regular season.

The result? Sunday’s finale against the Royals is already lined up as a bullpen day with Spencer Arrighetti as the “bulk guy”, either starting or following an opener. That was a fine enough plan for one spot in the rotation, but if the Blue Jays have two up in the air, this bullpen -- which is already running on fumes -- will be asked to carry the team.
The latest on Trey Yesavage
The Taillon news makes Yesavage’s timeline even more important.
The 23-year-old threw 23 pitches in a bullpen session Friday at the club’s complex in Dunedin, Fla., and felt fine. He was up to 92 mph in that session and is scheduled to throw another on Monday.

If all goes well, the Blue Jays would then get Yesavage on the mound facing some hitters at the complex on Thursday, simulating roughly two innings. It’s possible he pitches in a Minor League rehab game after that or continues to face hitters in a more controlled environment at the complex, but either way, it’s beginning to feel like Yesavage has a real shot to come back and help, even if he’d be pitching in shorter bursts.
items.author: Keegan Matheson

items.titleEn: Blue Jays back to .500 and in thick of AL Wild Card race
bodyEn: KANSAS CITY -- Finally back to .500, the Blue Jays have 20 games to determine how we’ll remember the 2026 season and they’re playing their best baseball at exactly the right time.​

This isn’t the race the Blue Jays dreamed of when they entered the 2026 season as World Series contenders, fresh off taking the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7, but none of that matters now. The Blue Jays have given themselves another life, and with Friday’s 9-2 win over the Royals, are back to .500 (71-71). This leaves them just one game shy of the Guardians, who they hold a tiebreaker over.
“We’re gritty as hell,” said Ernie Clement. “If we go down early, we’re not afraid to come back. Right now, we’re punching first, which is something I don’t think we had done early in the season.”
This is what mattered most:
1. Another offensive outburst
This hasn’t been the Blue Jays’ “brand of baseball” by any means, but what a start Friday night.

With a flurry of blows right out of the gate, the Blue Jays hung four runs on the Royals in the first inning, capped by an Ernie Clement double into the left-field corner. This was a Clement classic, and much-needed after he’s been grinding through the past month offensively.

"The boys have done a great job picking me up after my historic month of August,” Clement joked. “These guys are awesome. We're playing great baseball. It’s not about me, so I’ve got to put my frustrations aside and try to help the team win. It felt good to get a couple, score a run, a couple of RBIs, just be part of a win.”

No one is going to mistake the 2026 Blue Jays for an offensive powerhouse, but with performances like this and the growing belief that Vladimir Guerrero Jr. could finally be turning a corner, there’s at least some optimism. Slowly and steadily, John Schneider has seen this grow since the Trade Deadline.

“Our at-bats have definitely been better and we’ve gotten some timely hitting,” Schneider said. “We got a lot of hits in the month of August as a team. We’re doing the little things better. We’re playing better defense. We’re keeping games where they should be better than we did at the beginning of the year. Then, the offense has kind of picked up a little bit.”
2. Key conversations around the Trade Deadline

The Blue Jays were trying to “thread the needle”. It’s so rare that teams actually pull that off, but with additions like José Soriano and the immediate impact of prospect returns like Brett Bateman, it’s working.

Leading up to that Deadline, Schneider and general manager Ross Atkins sought out players they knew would be sticking around and had some very direct, daily conversations with them. They wanted to get out in front of it.

“We really wanted to say that every day to the guys. ‘Hey, we still believe that a lot of you guys can be better and we’re just going to sell our entire [freaking] roster. We’re going to continue to compete,’” Schneider said. “I think that saying that every single day was important. Then, it was the guys believing that and going out and playing with it. That’s what we were trying to do.”
It’s taken some patience, but this is the vision the Blue Jays had all along.

“We’re a really good baseball team,” Clement said. “It was only a matter of time before things started clicking and we started playing our game, figured out our team identity, figured out our lineup. There’s been so many moving pieces throughout the whole year. It’s nice to finally have a solid grasp on who we are.”
3. The path forward

This weekend won’t get any easier for the Blue Jays after Jameson Taillon left Friday’s game following the second inning with right elbow discomfort. This bullpen, already running on fumes, needed to cover seven innings. There’s essentially another “bullpen day” around Spencer Arrighetti as the bulk guy on Sunday, too.

There can be no complaining from the driver’s seat, though. With the Guardians playing a motivated Tigers team, the Rangers playing the Rays and the Orioles playing the Red Sox, this weekend is wide open for the Blue Jays to separate themselves in the AL Wild Card race before some more winnable games against the A’s.

items.titleEn: All 30 teams set to open Spring Training 2027 on same day
bodyEn: Major League Baseball announced the 2027 Spring Training schedule on Friday.
All 30 MLB teams in Arizona’s Cactus League and Florida’s Grapefruit League will open Spring Training on Feb. 19.

Some of the first-day matchups include the Dodgers and White Sox facing off at their shared facility at Camelback Ranch in Glendale, Ariz., and the Yankees traveling to Dunedin, Fla., to play the Blue Jays.

As usual, the Spring Training schedule also features exhibition games at MLB parks. The Freeway Series will take place from March 21-23 -- the first game will be at Dodger Stadium on March 21 and the last two will be played at Angel Stadium.
Additionally, we’ll also see the Rays host the Blue Jays at Tropicana Field on March 20, as well as the Tigers on March 21 and 23.

The 2027 regular season will get underway on Wednesday, March 24, with an Opening Night game presented by Adobe, live on Netflix. That matchup will be announced at a later date. A day later, the traditional Opening Day presented by Adobe will feature 14 games, including a primetime matchup on NBC (the opponents for that game has yet to be determined).
